newsitem.title: USA: More competition seen ahead for U.S. ag exports.
newsitem.headline: More competition seen ahead for U.S. ag exports.

text.p: U.S. corn and wheat exports will meet tough competition in the months ahead, but the outlook for soybeans and soybean products looks good, the Agriculture Department said Thursday.

In a report that was only mildly surprising to commodity traders and analysts, government experts raised wheat and corn production estimates in many key non-U.S. producing areas and boosted their projections for soybean demand in key markets for U.S. farmers.
Soybean prices at the Chicago Board of Trade posted gains in reaction to the favourable outlook, helping to support corn and wheat futures.

U.S. soybean exports for this marketing year beginning Sept. 1 -- which have already been running well ahead of last year's rate -- should continue their good pace at least for the next few months due to booming demand from China, the European Union, Mexico and Thailand.

But corn exports, the biggest export crop of American farmers, are expected to tighten this winter and spring because of good foreign crops and less demand for imports in Brazil, Hungary, Mexico and other importing nations, the department said.

U.S. farmers generally provide over 70 percent of the almost 67 million metric tons of corn traded in world markets. But that hold on the markets can weaken with good crops in other countries and good harvests of alternative crops such as barley and sorghum.

"With corn, you just can't look at corn -- for instance, barley is better this year than last," said Mike Helmar, senior economist for The WEFA Group, an economic consulting firm near Philadelphia. "And since we control so much of the corn market, U.S. corn more quickly feels any change in supply/demand around the world," he said.

U.S. wheat exports -- already projected to be down sharply from last year's high levels -- were left unchanged, but wheat production estimates were raised for Australia, Argentina and Canada. Experts said that indicated more aggressive export campaigns from those countries and probably a further downward adjustment in U.S. wheat exports.
"It's going to be much more competitive for the United States," said Helmar.

He and others said not only will it be tough going for U.S. wheat exports near term, but they warned that next year's wheat crop is also likely to have a harder time than normal in finding eager buyers.
"As we approach summer and the new (wheat) crop, foreign suppliers will still have supplies to sell," said Paul Dickerson, vice president of U.S. Wheat Associates, a major wheat producer group.
